title: Given a Scenario, Implement Workstation Backup and Recovery Methods

sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: A backup is useful only when the correct data was copied, the copy can be restored, and enough separated copies exist to survive the failure being addressed.
sections.callout: Copy it → store it safely → test it → restore it.

sections.title: Maestro Focus
paragraphs: Identify the backup type, the restore destination, the required backup sets, and the rotation or copy strategy that best protects the workstation's data.

sections.title: Backup
paragraphs: Backups protect against hardware failure, accidental deletion, corruption, malware, ransomware, device loss, and disaster. The protected copy must be separate enough that the same event does not destroy the original and every backup.

sections.title: Full Backup
paragraphs: A full backup copies all selected data. It typically requires the most time and storage but provides the simplest restore because the complete selected set is together.
sections.callout: Everything selected is copied → full backup.

sections.title: Incremental Backup
paragraphs: An incremental backup copies changes since the most recent backup of any type. It is usually small and fast.
bullets: Restore the last full backup
Then restore every incremental created after that full
sections.callout: Changes since the last backup → incremental.

sections.title: Differential Backup
paragraphs: A differential backup copies all changes since the most recent full backup. Each differential grows until the next full backup.
bullets: Restore the last full backup
Then restore only the latest differential
sections.callout: Changes since the last full → differential.

sections.title: Full, Incremental, and Differential Comparison

table.caption: Compare backup and recovery tradeoffs
rows: Changes since the last backup of any type
Last full plus every later incremental

sections.callout: Incremental → last anything; differential → last full.

sections.title: Synthetic Full Backup
paragraphs: A synthetic full creates a new full backup by combining previously stored backup data rather than rereading every selected file from the original workstation.
sections.callout: Original source data → full; existing backup sets → synthetic full.

sections.title: Recovery
paragraphs: Creating copies is only half the process. Recovery returns protected information to a usable state and location.

sections.title: In-Place/Overwrite and Alternative Location

entries.title: In-Place/Overwrite
paragraphs: Restores data to its original location and may replace the current version.

entries.title: Alternative Location
paragraphs: Restores data somewhere else so versions can be compared, current files remain untouched, recovered data can be inspected, or an unavailable original location can be bypassed.

sections.callout: Replace at the original destination → in-place; preserve and inspect elsewhere → alternative location.

sections.title: Backup Testing
paragraphs: A successful backup job does not prove recovery will work. Test restores verify backup integrity, required data, access permissions, recovery steps, and recovery time.
sections.callout: A backup never restored is an unproven backup.

sections.title: Frequency
paragraphs: Backup and test frequency should match data importance, rate of change, risk, and how much work the organization can afford to recreate. Regular backups require regular restore testing.

sections.title: Backup Rotation Schemes
paragraphs: Rotation defines how multiple backup generations and copies are maintained over time and across locations or media.

sections.title: Onsite vs. Offsite

entries.title: Onsite
paragraphs: Local backups can be accessed quickly but may be destroyed by the same fire, flood, theft, or building-wide incident as production systems.

entries.title: Offsite
paragraphs: Geographically separated backups provide resilience when the primary location is lost.

sections.callout: Fast local access → onsite; geographic separation → offsite.

sections.title: Grandfather-Father-Son (GFS)
paragraphs: GFS retains several generations, commonly daily son backups, weekly father backups, and monthly grandfather backups. Older generations help when corruption is discovered after recent copies are already affected.

sections.title: 3-2-1 Backup Rule
paragraphs: Maintain three copies of the data on two different media or storage types, with one copy stored offsite.
bullets: Original workstation data
Local backup on a different system or medium
Offsite or cloud backup

sections.title: GFS vs. 3-2-1
paragraphs: GFS describes generations retained over time. The 3-2-1 rule describes copy count, media diversity, and location. A backup plan can use both.
sections.callout: When generations come from → GFS; how many copies and where they live → 3-2-1.

sections.title: Backup Strategy Example
bullets: Sunday: full backup
Monday through Saturday: incremental backups
Local onsite copy for quick recovery
Secondary offsite copy for disaster resilience
Monthly archival copy retained through GFS
Regular test restores to verify recovery

sections.title: Recognition Cues
bullets: Everything copied → full
Changes since last backup → incremental
Changes since last full → differential
New full built from stored backup sets → synthetic full
Restore to original location → in-place or overwrite
Restore somewhere else → alternative location
Prove data can be restored → backup testing
How often backups or tests occur → frequency
Backup stored locally → onsite
Backup stored elsewhere → offsite
Daily, weekly, and monthly generations → GFS
Three copies, two media, one offsite → 3-2-1

sections.title: Objective 4.3 Exam Trap
bullets: Incremental copies changes since the last backup; differential copies changes since the last full.
Incremental recovery needs the full plus every later incremental; differential recovery needs the full plus the latest differential.
A full reads original source data; a synthetic full builds from existing backup information.
Backup creates the protected copy; recovery restores it.
In-place uses the original destination; alternative location uses a different destination.
A completed backup job is not proof until a restore is tested.
GFS means daily, weekly, and monthly generations; 3-2-1 means three copies, two media types, and one offsite.

sections.title: Maestro Recognition Sheet
bullets: Everything → full
Since last backup → incremental
Since last full → differential
Full made from backup data → synthetic full
Original location → in-place restore
Different location → alternative restore
Prove restore works → backup testing
How often → frequency
Same location → onsite
Different geographic location → offsite
Daily, weekly, monthly → GFS
Three copies, two media, one offsite → 3-2-1
sections.callout: Copy it → store it safely → test it → restore it.
